Differential Signaling Workflow

Source: vignettes/differential_signaling.Rmd
differential_signaling.Rmd

In this tutorial, we will walk through the workflow for performing differential signaling analysis using the dominoSignal package. While the other tutorials focus on signaling networks inferred from a single data set, many studies involve multiple subjects or conditions, requiring the comparison of signaling across these groups. The dominoSignal package implements the Differential Cell Signaling Test (DCST), a framework for identifying receptor, ligand, and transcription factor (TF) linkages that are significantly differentially present across groups of subjects. This method is described in detail in Differential cell signaling testing for cell-cell communication inference from single-cell data by dominoSignal (2026) published in Bioinformatics. The publication also includes simulation benchmarking and application of the method to pancreatic cancer and immunotherapy data sets. Refer to the publication for full details on the method and biological validation of the workflow.

Workflow overview

The differential signaling workflow consists of the following steps:

  1. Build a domino() object per subject to be compared (see the Getting Started tutorial for details on building a domino() object).
  2. Compile linkages across the subjects into a linkage_summary object using the summarize_linkages() function.
  3. [Optional] Subset the linkage_summary object to include only the subjects of interest.
  4. Create a table of linkage observations within groups of subjects using the count_linkage() function.
  5. Test differences in linkage frequency across groups using the test_differential_linkages() function, which implements a Fisher’s exact test.
  6. Visualize the results using the plot_differential_linkages() function.

The DCST workflow can be performed with 2 or more groups of subjects. In this tutorial, we will demonstrate the workflow for both a two-group comparison (condition A vs condition B) and a comparison across more than two groups.

Demonstration data

In this tutorial, we use the domino() object built in the Getting Started tutorial. If you have not yet built a domino() object, you can do so by following the instructions on that page or use the code below to load the pre-built domino() object.

Instructions to load data 
set.seed(42)
library(dominoSignal)
library(dplyr)
library(kableExtra)

# BiocFileCache helps with file management across sessions
bfc <- BiocFileCache::BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE)
data_url <- "https://zenodo.org/records/10951634/files/pbmc_domino_built.rds"
tmp_path <- BiocFileCache::bfcrpath(bfc, data_url)
dom <- readRDS(tmp_path)

Because the differential signaling workflow compares linkages across multiple domino() objects (one per subject), we will create six synthetic domino() objects from the same PBMC dataset. For each synthetic subject, we randomly retain a subset of the cells without replacement while keeping their true cluster labels and then perturb the cluster labels of a subset of those cells by reshuffling within that subset. This approach preserves some amount of per-cluster signaling while making sure each domino() object is distinct from the others, giving the example workflow something to compare.1

Note that reshuffling is only for demonstration purposes and does not represent any biological differences. In practice, you would build one domino() object from each biological subject or sample to be used in the comparison. To ensure results are comparable across subjects, use the same parameters in create_domino() and build_domino() for all subjects. Refer to the DCST publication for an example of this workflow applied to real data.

Creating synthetic replicates

To start, we extract the inputs from the original domino() object so we can supply them to the create_domino() function for the synthetic subjects.

rl_map <- dom_database(dom, name_only = FALSE)
features <- dom_tf_activation(dom)
# Access counts slot directly to maintain sparse matrix format
counts <- slot(dom, "counts")
zscores <- dom_zscores(dom)
tf_targets <- dom_linkages(dom, link_type = "tf-target")
clusters <- dom_clusters(dom, labels = TRUE)

We can use a helper function to resample the cells and shuffle the cluster labels for a subset of them, and then rebuild the domino() object with create_domino() and build_domino() using the same parameters across all subjects so that they can be compared.2

build_reps <- function(clusters, seed, keep_frac, shuffle_frac) {
    # Local seed for reproducibility without affecting global seed
    withr::with_seed(seed, {
        n_cells <- length(clusters)
        keep_cells <- sort(sample.int(n_cells, size = round(n_cells * keep_frac),
            replace = FALSE))

        resampled_clusters <- clusters[keep_cells]
        features <- features[, keep_cells, drop = FALSE]
        counts <- counts[, keep_cells, drop = FALSE]
        zscores <- zscores[, keep_cells, drop = FALSE]
        shuffled_idx <- sample(seq_along(resampled_clusters), size = round(shuffle_frac *
            length(resampled_clusters)), replace = FALSE)

        resampled_clusters[shuffled_idx] <- sample(resampled_clusters[shuffled_idx])

        dom_shuffle <- create_domino(rl_map = rl_map, features = features, counts = counts,
            z_scores = zscores, clusters = resampled_clusters, tf_targets = tf_targets,
            use_complexes = TRUE, remove_rec_dropout = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

        dom_shuffle <- build_domino(dom = dom_shuffle, max_tf_pval = 0.05, max_tf_per_clust = 25,
            max_rec_per_tf = 25, rec_tf_cor_threshold = 0.1, min_rec_percentage = 0.05)
    })

    return(dom_shuffle)
}

params <- data.frame(set = c(161803, 314159, 6631034, 6021023, 831446, 98067), keep = c(0.95,
    0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 0.9, 0.9), shuffle = c(0.15, 0.1, 0.15, 0.1, 0.15, 0.1))

# This does take a few minutes to run
dom_list <- purrr::pmap(params, function(set, keep, shuffle) {
    build_reps(clusters, seed = set, keep_frac = keep, shuffle_frac = shuffle)
})

names(dom_list) <- paste0("P", seq_along(dom_list))

We now have six domino() objects that we can treat as different subjects (P1-6).

The linkage_summary class

The linkage_summary() class is the structure used for the differential signaling workflow. It contains linkages present in each cluster across the domino() objects it contains, along with subject metadata. The object contains three slots:

  • subject_names: a factor with a unique name for each subject (domino() object) represented in the summary.
  • subject_meta: a data frame with one row per subject including provided metadata (such as condition, treatment, or other covariates) that can be used to group or subset subjects for comparison.
  • subject_linkages: a nested list organized as subject to cluster to linkage type (tfs for active transcription factors, rec for active receptors, incoming_lig for ligands that can activate the cluster, tfs_rec for transcription factor to receptor pairs, and rec_lig for receptor to ligand pairs).

To create a linkage_summary() object, we use the summarize_linkages() function, which takes a named list of domino() objects and a data frame of subject metadata. The first column of the data frame must contain subject names that match the names of the domino() objects in the list.

subject_metas <- data.frame(patient = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P5", "P6"), time = c("pre",
    "post", "pre", "post", "pre", "post"), condition = c("control", "treatment",
    "treatment", "control", "control", "control"), batch = c("A", "A", "B", "B",
    "C", "C"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

link_summary <- summarize_linkages(dom_list, subject_metas, subject_names = subject_metas$patient)

print(link_summary)
#> A linkage summary object of 6 subjects with 4 metadata annotations and linkages between 9 clusters.

The print and show methods for the linkage_summary() class report the number of subjects, the number of metadata annotations, and the number of clusters present in the summary.

Since we built this linkage summary from six domino() objects with six distinct groups and two distinct conditions, we can subset the summary to include only the subjects of interest.

To create a comparison for only the treatment condition, we can subset the linkage_summary() object by the relevant metadata column.

link_treat <- subset(link_summary, subset = condition == "treatment")
print(link_treat)
#> A linkage summary object of 2 subjects with 4 metadata annotations and linkages between 9 clusters.

Subjects can also be selected by name or with compound expressions.

subset(link_summary, subset = subject_names %in% c("P1", "P3"))
#> A linkage summary object of 2 subjects with 4 metadata annotations and linkages between 9 clusters.
subset(link_summary, subset = condition == "treatment" | time == "pre")
#> A linkage summary object of 4 subjects with 4 metadata annotations and linkages between 9 clusters.

As an alternative to creating separate subset objects, the other functions in the differential signaling workflow accept a subject_names argument that can be used to restrict the subjects considered in the analysis without needing to create a separate linkage_summary object.

Counting linkages across groups

The count_linkage() function tabulates the number of subjects with a given linkage in a specified cluster, which can also be broken down by a metadata column. The linkage argument selects which of the linkage types to count.

Total counts

If no grouping variable is specified and no subject names are provided, the function will return a data frame with the total number of subjects with each linkage in the selected cluster.

count_all <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "CD8_T_cell", linkage = "rec_lig") %>%
    slice_sample(n = 5)
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(count_all, caption = "Total counts of receptor-ligand linkages in CD8 T Cells"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
Total counts of receptor-ligand linkages in CD8 T Cells
feature total_count
TNFRSF1B <- LTA 1
CD2 <- CD58 6
LAMP1 <- FAM3C 6
CXCR3 <- CXCL11 6
TNFRSF1B <- GRN 1

If specific subjects are of interest, the counts can be restricted to those subjects by providing a vector of the subject names.

count_subjects <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "CD8_T_cell", linkage = "tfs",
    subject_names = c("P1", "P2"))
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(count_subjects[1:5, ], caption = "Subset of counts of TF linkages in patients P1 & P2 in CD8 T Cells"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
Subset of counts of TF linkages in patients P1 & P2 in CD8 T Cells

CHURC1 1
CREM 2

Grouped counts

The count_linkage() function can also return counts that are grouped by a metadata column. For example, we can count the linkages for subjects in the treatment condition grouped by the “time” column to see how many subjects in each time point have each linkage.

counts_time_trt <- count_linkage(link_treat, cluster = "CD14_monocyte", linkage = "tfs_rec",
    group.by = "time")
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(slice_sample(counts_time_trt, n = 5), caption = "Counts of TF-Receptor linkages in CD14 Monocytes grouped by time for treatment subjects"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
Counts of TF-Receptor linkages in CD14 Monocytes grouped by time for treatment subjects
feature total_count post pre
CEBPE <- TNFRSF1A 2 1 1
CEBPA <- CSF1R 2 1 1
CEBPE <- CSF1R 2 1 1
IRF8 <- TNFRSF1B 2 1 1
ATF3 <- TNFRSF1A 2 1 1

This is equivalent to grouping by the “time” column and providing the subject names of only the subjects in the treatment condition.

counts_time_subj <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "CD14_monocyte", linkage = "tfs_rec",
    group.by = "time", subject_names = c("P2", "P3"))
identical(counts_time_trt, counts_time_subj)
#> [1] TRUE

Of course, more than one subject can be in each group, and the counts will reflect the number of subjects in each group with each linkage.

counts_condition <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "naive_CD4_T_cell", linkage = "incoming_lig",
    group.by = "condition") %>%
    slice_sample(n = 5)
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(counts_condition, caption = "Counts of incoming ligand linkages in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by condition"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
Counts of incoming ligand linkages in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by condition
feature total_count control treatment
DHCR24 6 4 2
CD70 6 4 2
CDH1 6 4 2
IL7 6 4 2
PTGES2 1 1 0

And more than two groups can be compared at once.

counts_batch <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "CD14_monocyte", linkage = "rec",
    group.by = "batch") %>%
    slice_sample(n = 5)
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(counts_batch, caption = "Counts of receptor linkages in CD14 Monocytes grouped by batch"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

Testing differential linkages

The count_linkage() function tabulates the number of subjects with a given linkage in a specified cluster, but it does not test whether the frequency of that linkage is significantly different across groups. The test_differential_linkages() function uses a contingency table of presence/absence of each linkage across groups to perform a Fisher’s exact test. The p-values across all tested linkages are adjusted for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate method.

The test_differential_linkages() function returns a data frame that includes the cluster, linkage, grouping variable, test name (always fisher’s exact test), the linkage being compared, the test statistics (odds ratio, if applicable, and p-value, both raw and adjusted), total number of subjects where linkage is active, number of subjects in each group where linkage is active, number of total subjects compared, and the total number of subjects in each group.

Two-group comparisons

When exactly two groups are compared, the fisher.test() function returns an odds ratio in addition to the p-value, reflecting the relative odds of the linkage being present in one group compared to the other.

dcst_time_trt <- test_differential_linkages(link_treat, cluster = "CD14_monocyte",
    linkage = "tfs_rec", group.by = "time")
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(slice_sample(dcst_time_trt, n = 5), caption = "DCST of TF-Receptor linkages in CD14 Monocytes grouped by time for treatment subjects"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
DCST of TF-Receptor linkages in CD14 Monocytes grouped by time for treatment subjects
cluster linkage group.by test_name feature odds.ratio p.value p.adj total_count post_count pre_count total_n post_n pre_n
ZNF77 <- CD36 CD14_monocyte tfs_rec time fishers.exact ZNF77 <- CD36 0 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1
FOSB <- CD86 CD14_monocyte tfs_rec time fishers.exact FOSB <- CD86 0 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1
FOSL1 <- TNFRSF1B CD14_monocyte tfs_rec time fishers.exact FOSL1 <- TNFRSF1B 0 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1
KLF4 <- FcRn_complex CD14_monocyte tfs_rec time fishers.exact KLF4 <- FcRn_complex Inf 1 1 1 1 0 2 1 1
ZNF516 <- FCGR2A CD14_monocyte tfs_rec time fishers.exact ZNF516 <- FCGR2A 0 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1

As with the count_linkage() function, the same results can be obtained by providing the subject names of only the subjects in the treatment condition.

dcst_time_subj <- test_differential_linkages(link_summary, cluster = "CD14_monocyte",
    linkage = "tfs_rec", group.by = "time", subject_names = c("P2", "P3"))
identical(dcst_time_trt, dcst_time_subj)
#> [1] TRUE

The test_differential_linkages() function does require that any grouping variable has at least two groups with at least one subject in each group.

test_differential_linkages(link_treat, cluster = "CD14_monocyte", linkage = "tfs_rec",
    group.by = "condition")
#> Error in `test_differential_linkages()`:
#> ! At least 2 groups of condition must be represented among the included subjects; found: treatment

It is obviously preferable to have more than one subject in each group (though the function does return results for groups with only one subject). Note that there are no significant differences between the groups in this example, which is expected since the subjects were generated from the same data set.

dcst_time <- test_differential_linkages(link_summary, cluster = "CD8_T_cell", linkage = "rec",
    group.by = "time") %>%
    dplyr::arrange(desc(odds.ratio))
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(slice_sample(dcst_time, n = 5), caption = "DCST of receptor-ligand linkages in CD8 T Cells grouped by time"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
DCST of receptor-ligand linkages in CD8 T Cells grouped by time
cluster linkage group.by test_name feature odds.ratio p.value p.adj total_count post_count pre_count total_n post_n pre_n

SORL1 CD8_T_cell rec time fishers.exact SORL1 0 1 1 6 3 3 6 3 3
CD8_receptor CD8_T_cell rec time fishers.exact CD8_receptor 0 1 1 6 3 3 6 3 3
CXCR4 CD8_T_cell rec time fishers.exact CXCR4 0 1 1 6 3 3 6 3 3

Multi-group comparisons

When more than two groups are compared, the fisher.test() function does not return an odds ratio (so it is set to NA in the DCST output), but the p-value still reflects whether the frequency of the linkage is significantly different across groups.

dcst_batch <- test_differential_linkages(link_summary, cluster = "naive_CD4_T_cell",
    linkage = "rec", group.by = "batch") %>%
    arrange(p.value)
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(slice_sample(dcst_batch, n = 5), caption = "DCST of receptors in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by batch"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
DCST of receptors in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by batch
cluster linkage group.by test_name feature odds.ratio p.value p.adj total_count A_count B_count C_count total_n A_n B_n C_n

PTGER2 naive_CD4_T_cell rec batch fishers.exact PTGER2 NA 1 1 1 0 0 1 6 2 2 2
TNFRSF25 naive_CD4_T_cell rec batch fishers.exact TNFRSF25 NA 1 1 6 2 2 2 6 2 2 2
RORA naive_CD4_T_cell rec batch fishers.exact RORA NA 1 1 6 2 2 2 6 2 2 2
HLA-C naive_CD4_T_cell rec batch fishers.exact HLA-C NA 1 1 6 2 2 2 6 2 2 2

There is no limit to the number of groups that can be compared at once (as long as there is at least one subject in each group).

dcst_patient <- test_differential_linkages(link_summary, cluster = "naive_CD4_T_cell",
    linkage = "rec_lig", group.by = "patient") %>%
    arrange(p.value)
Show table code 
kableExtra::kable_styling(knitr::kable(slice_sample(dcst_patient, n = 5), caption = "DCST of receptor-ligand linkages in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by patient"),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
DCST of receptor-ligand linkages in naive CD4 T Cells grouped by patient

NCR3 <- NCR3LG1 naive_CD4_T_cell rec_lig patient fishers.exact NCR3 <- NCR3LG1 NA 1 1 5 1 1 1 0 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 1
ICOS <- TNF naive_CD4_T_cell rec_lig patient fishers.exact ICOS <- TNF NA 1 1 5 0 1 1 1 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 1
LAMP1 <- FAM3C naive_CD4_T_cell rec_lig patient fishers.exact LAMP1 <- FAM3C NA 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 1
NCR3 <- BAG6 naive_CD4_T_cell rec_lig patient fishers.exact NCR3 <- BAG6 NA 1 1 5 1 1 1 0 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 1

The DCST paper includes additional information on the recommended number of subjects for robust results (ideally at least 15 per group), as well as an approach to simulate biological replicates using bootstrapping of cells for experiments with small numbers of replicates (scripts for the manuscript can be found at the corresponding GitHub repository).

Visualizing differential linkages

In order to visualize the results of the DCST, the plot_differential_linkages() function can be used to create a heatmap of the test statistic along with row-level bar plots showing the proportions of subjects in which linkages are active.

The function has arguments for the test statistic (the column of the DCST result that contains the statistic to be plotted), the range of values to be plotted, the heatmap gradient, and the color palette to use for the groups being compared.

Two-group comparisons

An example of a two-group comparison is shown below, where the p-value is used as the test statistic and rows are ordered by ascending p-value. All p-values are 1 in this example, so every cell shows the maximum gradient color.

plot_differential_linkages(differential_linkages = slice_sample(dcst_time_trt, n = 15),
    test_statistic = "p.value", stat_range = c(0, 1), stat_ranking = "ascending")

plot_differential_linkages(differential_linkages = slice_sample(dcst_time, n = 15),
    test_statistic = "p.value", gradient = c(minimum = "#c44f4f", maximum = "#ffd771"),
    stat_ranking = "ascending")

If comparing between two groups, it is also possible to use the odds ratio as the test statistic, which will show the relative odds of a linkage being present in one group compared to the other.

plot_differential_linkages(differential_linkages = slice_sample(dcst_time, n = 15),
    test_statistic = "odds.ratio", stat_range = c(0, 4), stat_ranking = "descending",
    gradient = c(minimum = "gray90", maximum = "orange"))

Multi-group comparisons

When comparing between more than two groups, the odds ratio is not available, so the p-value (or adjusted p-value) is the only option for the test statistic.

plot_differential_linkages(differential_linkages = slice_sample(dcst_batch, n = 15),
    test_statistic = "p.value", stat_range = c(0, 1), stat_ranking = "ascending",
    gradient = c(minimum = "#ff4c43", maximum = "#ffe6c0"))

A custom color can be assigned to each group’s barplot annotation using the group_palette argument, which takes a named vector of colors where names correspond to the group names in the DCST result.

plot_differential_linkages(differential_linkages = slice_sample(dcst_batch, n = 15),
    test_statistic = "p.value", stat_range = c(0, 1), stat_ranking = "ascending",
    gradient = c(minimum = "#7b43ff", maximum = "#c0c5ff"), group_palette = c(A = "#64a5e6",
        B = "#71fcad", C = "#c968c3"))

This can be useful for consistency across multiple plots or to match publication color schemes.

Example run

Here’s an example of what a workflow might look like from the list of domino() objects to the final visualization of differential linkages. We begin with the list of synthetic domino() objects created above, create the metadata, create a link_summary() object, examine the counts for the linkages,and then run the DCST for a comparison by batch. In this example, we focus on incoming ligands in the CD14 monocyte cluster.

subject_metas <- data.frame(patient = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P5", "P6"), time = c("pre",
    "post", "pre", "post", "pre", "post"), condition = c("control", "treatment",
    "treatment", "control", "control", "control"), batch = c("A", "A", "B", "B",
    "C", "C"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

link_summary <- summarize_linkages(dom_list, subject_metas, subject_names = subject_metas$patient)

counts_batch <- count_linkage(link_summary, cluster = "CD14_monocyte", linkage = "incoming_lig",
    group.by = "batch")

dcst_batch <- test_differential_linkages(link_summary, cluster = "CD14_monocyte",
    linkage = "incoming_lig", group.by = "batch")

plot_differential_linkages(dcst_batch, test_statistic = "p.value", stat_ranking = "ascending",
    gradient = c(minimum = "#e02c2c", maximum = "#feffcd"), group_palette = c(A = "#2a6aaa",
        B = "#07bd56", C = "#a244a3"))
